1:
The prophet is sent down from the temple to the palace, and Gill and Calvin both take the word literally: he was on the temple mount, from which there was a descent to the king's house. Which king he faced is disputed. Gill names Jehoiakim as then reigning. Clarke reports the view that the oracle belongs to the first year of Zedekiah and reads the servants addressed as the ministers who had counselled that king to rebel; Henry likewise sets it against the embassy of the preceding chapter. Ellicott proposes that the message, delivered in the palace to the reigning king, reviews the three preceding reigns and reproduces the very words of the warnings given in each, all by then too terribly fulfilled; and that the phrase about the throne implies the king sat in the gate before his people.

Henry states the principle in a sentence: subjects must own that where the word of the king is there is power over them, but kings must own that where the word of the Lord is there is power over them. Calvin says the throne of David is named not to honour its occupant but to aggravate his guilt, that throne being priestly and a type of the kingdom afterwards revealed in Christ, so that a degenerate heir is the less tolerable. Keil and Delitzsch put the charge plainly: the king is warned against injustice and the oppression of the defenceless, and told to save the despoiled from the oppressor.

The charge itself is worked over closely. Ellicott observes that the verb differs from the one used in the previous chapter and implies a less formal act, so the sense is do judgment rather than execute it, and that the Hebrew order throws the emphasis onto the violence forbidden; the verse paints only too vividly a reign that was the reverse of all it describes. Calvin distinguishes the pair: to do judgment is to condemn the guilty, to do justice to acquit the innocent, and the specification following takes them in reverse order, rescuing the plundered answering to justice and sparing the helpless to judgment. He explains why these three are always named: the orphan lacks wisdom, the widow strength, the stranger friends, and a judge unswayed by relations or wealth in their case proves his integrity conspicuously. It is bad, he adds, when the guilty go unpunished; worse when the helpless are oppressed and the innocent condemned. Henry puts the same in two rules, that they do all the good they can with their power and no hurt with it, the worst violence being that done under colour of law by those whose office is to prevent it.

On the promise attached, Henry reads a plain conditional: an uninterrupted succession in state and tranquillity, the most effectual way to preserve the dignity of government being to do the duty of it. Calvin will not let the offer stand so simply. The exile was already determined and had to be borne; repentance could still have secured a milder and shorter captivity, some form of the kingdom surviving, and a restoration at length, which is mitigation and not impunity. Ellicott notes that the chariots and horses reproduce an earlier promise and stand as the symbol of kingly pomp.

The threat is sworn. Ellicott calls the formula exceptionally rare and states the principle the Epistle to the Hebrews draws from it, that men swear by the greater while God can swear by nothing greater than himself; and he settles that the house doomed is the palace, not the Temple. Calvin explains the oath by human dullness, sinners being deaf until God penetrates their hearts by force, and it had seemed incredible that a family set apart from the world could perish. He notices too that the commission's single word has become words in the threat.
6:
The oracle turns to the royal house, which Gill takes for the family rather than the building, though he allows the phrase may be rendered concerning the house and so refer to the palace. What follows is a comparison, and the tile divides sharply over what it asserts. Clarke reports the suggestion that the words allude to the oaks and cedars out of which the palace was built, and reads it as compliment turned to threat: Lebanon was the highest mountain and Gilead the most fertile part of the country, fit emblems of the reigning family, and the God who raised them up can bring them down. Wesley works from the same geography, recalling that Gilead was begged of Moses by the tribes whose wealth lay in cattle, and supposes the palace compared to these places for its nobleness or pleasantness.

Ellicott sharpens the figure rather than the flattery. The conjunction is absent from the Hebrew and better dropped, and even in his woes the prophet's mind is still that of a poet: the point of comparison in both cases is the forest crowning the height, the oaks of the Gilead district being as famous as the cedars and both alike fit symbols of sovereign glory, with a possible glance at the cedar buildings that had given one palace the name of the house of the forest of Lebanon.

Calvin refuses all of this and says so, noting that interpreters differ and that he stands against them. Gilead is not a compliment here but a warning by precedent. The northern kingdom was by then wholly demolished and its people carried off, and Gilead stands by a part for that whole; the head of Lebanon is Jerusalem, as the felling of the cedars in the next verse shows. The sense is that Jerusalem shall be to God what Gilead already is, and he would have the future tense to make it plain. He dismisses the notion that Gilead was the chief city of the ten tribes, and remarks on the balsam for which the region was known and which the prophet had drawn on earlier in asking whether there was no medicine there to heal his people.

On the destroyers the voices converge. Gill points out that the Hebrew says the Lord will sanctify them, and draws from that not only appointment but an assurance that what they do by his order is consistent with his holiness. Clarke has God consecrating them to the work and giving their commission; Ellicott says the verb implies a solemn appointment. Calvin makes the point theologically, that the Chaldeans do not come of themselves, so the Jews were not contending with mortals but summoned to account; and he collates the versions, which render the verb as bringing, sanctifying, preparing and commissioning, and argues that the noun for their equipment means an implement of any kind, so hatchet suits better than weapon.

What the cedars are is disputed again. Ellicott carries the metaphor into persons and makes them the princes of the royal house with the chief counsellors and generals, as well as the columns of cedar wood. Clarke keeps a forest scene, a multitude of fellers each with his axe and no resistance offered, standing for the country's destruction. Calvin leaves it open between the cedar-panelled chambers and the trees of the mountain, taking the word either way for whatever was splendid in the city. On the travellers who ask why, Clarke thinks the words borrowed from the curses of Deuteronomy, Gill has the answer supplied by someone acquainted with the people's history. Calvin finds two contrasts in it, mortal men set against God and many nations against the one God, and turns it into a reproach: the heathen show more understanding than those forewarned who would not hear, and the covenant named in the answer removes any plea of ignorance.
10:
Ellicott marks this verse as where the detailed review of the three previous reigns begins, the prophecies reproduced as they were actually delivered. Almost everyone reads the dead as Josiah and the departing one as his successor. Gill sets aside the identification of the dead with Jehoiakim and names Josiah, greatly lamented, now to be wept for less because it is well with him and worse things remain. Ellicott recalls the dirge the prophet had composed for him, repeated on the anniversary of his death, and judges the doom of an exile who would never return a fitter subject for lamentation than the death of a righteous king taken from the evil to come. Wesley puts it in a line: Josiah is happy and needs no trouble taken for him. Henry adds that dying saints may be justly envied while living sinners are justly pitied, and that the prospect may grow so dismal that tears even for a Josiah must be reserved for ourselves.

Calvin will not have the verse tied to individuals. Others explain it of two named kings; he takes it for a general declaration about the whole people, since the prophet's point is that their condition would be such that it were better to die at once than protract life in continual languor. Ordinarily men dread death above exile, because the living may still emerge from their troubles while death cuts off hope; here the order is reversed, and exile becomes a slow infection, so that to die a hundred times would be more desirable. He allows a direct allusion to the dead king and the captive within the general sense, but insists the words be extended past the two. He notices also that the second verb means to nod, and that the head was shaken in scorn as readily as in condolence.

The name in the following verse divides them further. Gill rejects the identifications with Zedekiah and Jeconiah found in earlier commentators and settles on Jehoahaz. Clarke and Wesley agree, Clarke observing that Shallum was the name before the throne and Jehoahaz after it, as one brother became Jehoiakim and another Zedekiah. Ellicott presses why the private name is used: the throne name meant that the Lord sustains, while Shallum means retribution and might well have seemed a name of evil augury for a short and disastrous reign, with the further ill memory of a king of Israel of that name who reigned a single month. He notes that a Shallum stands fourth among the sons of Josiah in the genealogy, and suggests either an inverted order or two brothers of one name. Henry has the people making him king over an elder brother, so that his deposition within three months exposed the folly of their preference, and recalls the lament picturing him as a young lion caught and brought in chains to Egypt.

Calvin again stands alone, taking Shallum for Jeconiah, who gave up the kingdom and died in exile, meeting the difficulty that the text calls him son of Josiah by the Hebrew usage that names descendants sons. He draws from the verse the point he cares about most, that a pious ancestor shields nobody. Hypocrites make a defence out of their fathers' holiness and would have God bound by it, but Josiah's memory could not lessen the punishment of an heir who had degenerated, and the repetition that he reigned in his father's place is there to say so.

Keil and Delitzsch treat these two verses as closing the oracle and head what follows as the woe uttered upon Jehoiakim. On the last clause Ellicott argues from silence: the absence of the exile's name from the rest of the history is presumptive evidence that the prediction held, and there is no trace of his being alive even when the prophet was himself dragged down into that country.
13:
The woe falls on Jehoiakim, and the voices differ on what he did. Gill has him unwilling to keep the palace his predecessors used, building with money ill got and leaving workmen unpaid. Clarke notices that these charges are nowhere else circumstantially related and uses them to supply a mechanism: the history records that he taxed the land heavily to pay the Egyptian king, and this passage shows how, by taking the hirelings' wages and setting them to work for nothing. Ellicott sees the forced labour of Solomon's day revived, pressing this time not on resident foreigners but on Israelites, the unpaid labourers treated as slaves who, like their fathers in Egypt, got food and nothing more. He generalises the case to despotism itself, a king building palaces while his kingdom stood on the verge of ruin.

Calvin finds two distinct wrongs where the versions ran one together. His rendering makes the neighbour a slave for no cause, which is the wrong judgment, since a Hebrew might in some circumstances be reduced to service but here there was no ground; and then gives him nothing for his work, which is the injustice. He pushes a comparison further than anyone: a robber who kills at least takes the spoil, but the man who extorts a poor man's labour then sends him away naked and needy, and that is the more atrocious of the two.

Gill glosses the phrase as a house of dimensions. Ellicott finds the verb for cutting the windows to be the one used of dilating the eyes with antimony, so unusual width is meant; the vermilion he takes for the pigment still conspicuous in Egyptian buildings, and supposes the project driven by a vainglorious wish to imitate the king who had set Jehoiakim on his throne. Calvin says splendour in building cannot be condemned in itself, but that such appetite so seldom arises from anything but pride that the prophets denounced it with an eye to motive and end.

The taunt about cedar is read five ways. Gill takes it as false security, the wainscot no fortification but easily burnt. Clarke makes it self-importance, whether a man is a great king because he lives in a splendid house. Ellicott would render it that his ambition is in cedar, the verb meaning to vie, so that he is reproached for outdoing his greatest predecessors, and reports a variant behind the Greek making him vie with a named king. Keil and Delitzsch sharpen the question: it does not ask whether he will reign long but whether he supposes himself a king at all, since kingship consists in administering right and justice and not in raising palaces; and they dismiss the Greek variant as pointless. Calvin hears derision of a foolish confidence, a man painting walls when he had many dangers to dread, and adds that kings in his own day are ashamed to appear humane.

On the father the field converges. Ellicott takes the eating and drinking as praise of a healthy enjoyment, Josiah being no ascetic but a man who lived happily and did the true kingly work well. Calvin canvasses two other constructions before settling on the same sense, and rejects a rendering that would make the next verse an exhortation to the son, the verb being past. That the defence of the poor was itself knowledge of God is agreed by all: Ellicott says Josiah's fame rested less on restoring the Temple worship than on this; Wesley, that only those truly know God who obey him, and that men defective in justice and charity pretend to piety in vain; Calvin runs it backwards, that cruelty proves religion rooted out, since piety leads to all the duties of love. Against that Ellicott reads the son's covetousness as gain got by crushing, and traces the innocent blood to real killings, one of them a prophet's.
18:
Gill fixes the name first: Jehoiakim was Eliakim until the Egyptian king deposed his brother and set him up under a new one. Calvin adds that the patronymic is there not for honour but to touch him to the quick, since he had hoped his father's religion would cover him. The sentence is a funeral without mourners, and the cries quoted divide the tile. Clarke takes them for the burden of an actual dirge and points out that the last word is feminine and must mean the queen's glory. Calvin builds the same observation into a scheme: two cries bewail the dead king and two are condolence offered the surviving queen, whose glory departed with her husband. Ellicott hesitates, since sister would not be a fitting address to a king, and suggests instead a chorus of mourners, male and female, calling to one another. Keil and Delitzsch treat them as the formulas of hired mourners engaged for men and women alike, and note that the Greek found the sister objectionable and dropped her.

Clarke goes furthest afield to explain how such a refrain works, quoting a traveller's record of laments heard in India, a mother's for her child and a daughter's for her mother, every line closing on the same repeated cry, and concludes that the Hebrew dirges ended so.

Calvin enters a caution here that the others do not. Some suppose that nothing reported by a prophet can be other than approved, and take these lamentations for a pattern; but he is describing the custom of his age, as he had described royal chariots earlier without approving an ostentation kings had been forbidden. Left to himself Calvin thinks little of the practice: men vie with one another in grief, work themselves into a madness of crying, and when composed feign it, acting a part as in a theatre.

How the burial of an ass was carried out is not agreed. Keil and Delitzsch take the phrase for being left unburied in the open field or thrown into a flaying-ground, the body dragged out beyond the gates; Clarke likewise has him cast out, or buried without solemnity. Gill hears contempt in the choice of beast, a sordid and stupid creature and the king with it. Wesley reduces it to the essential, that none attended him and none mourned. Ellicott admits there is no direct record of the fulfilment, but observes that the prophet repeats the threat later in another form, and reconstructs the event: the king was dragged off in chains and probably died on the road, his corpse left as the army moved on. He adds that the formula about sleeping with his fathers cannot be pressed beyond the fact of dying, since it was used of a king who fell in battle. Calvin reconstructs it differently, supposing he died in fetters at Jerusalem before removal and was dragged out in the conqueror's indignation at his rebellion.

Calvin presses the participle: it means dragged, not carried, the body hauled out lest its stench infect the city, as one unworthy not only of a grave but of being looked at. Behind this he sets a doctrine of burial, that interment marks us off from beasts after death as we excel them in life, and is a pledge of immortality, the body hidden in the earth a mirror of a future life, so that to be denied it is a curse. Then he qualifies his own argument. Temporal punishments cannot always be read alike: God has let faithful servants lie unburied, the good share famine and war with the bad, and the prophet himself went into exile alongside the wicked, so outward circumstances often will not distinguish them. What the piling on of detail measures, he concludes, is the hardness of the hearers; a teachable king could have been told simply that he would not be buried.
20:
Why the three mountains are named divides the tile. Gill takes it as high ground from which Jerusalem may call to her neighbours for help, rejecting the reading that made Lebanon the temple; Henry has her crying from the rising ground as one undone. Clarke turns the geography into a route: these were the heights along the way by which the captives would be led out. Ellicott makes them witnesses that overlooked the invader's line of march, summoned as the hills of Gilboa once were, the people called from the counterfeit forest of their cedar palaces to the real mountains; and he prefers Abarim as a proper name. Wesley says they look toward the allies from whom help was expected, who are themselves in the conqueror's hand. Calvin declares the verse ironical: they were past counsel, so the prophet bids them howl to no purpose.

Calvin carries a figure through the passage that no one else presses. God is the husband, the neighbouring powers the lovers; the simplicity of faith is our spiritual chastity, so looking about for safety is adultery. On the reproach that follows he keeps the picture. A harsh husband may be disregarded with some excuse, but this one warned in time and confirmed his counsel by kindness, so the wife unmoved by both must be of a bad disposition. He notes that they never said in words that they would not obey, the prophet reading their life rather than their speech; and he refuses to soften the verb, since the complaint is that they would not so much as hear God's voice, much less obey it.

On the prosperity that bred this, Ellicott gives the literal plural and explains it by the old sense of security, the careless temper outward ease produces. Keil and Delitzsch take it much the same way and date the youth spoken of from the time the nation became God's people. Henry puts it in a proverb, that those who live at ease commonly live in contempt of the word, and makes it worse that the habit was inherited.

The threat against the shepherds turns on a pun three voices catch. Ellicott renders it that the wind shall feed on them that feed thee; Keil and Delitzsch say the verb was chosen for the play and compare the parching east wind that eats the grass, adding that the shepherds are all the authorities and not the same as the lovers; Calvin turns it back on the rulers, since the feeders had fed the people with wind and would now have nothing but wind to live on. He weighs whether they will find only emptiness to support them or be consumed by a blast, and prefers the first. Gill, Wesley and Clarke keep the plainer picture of rulers blasted as plants are. Calvin adds a political point: the people had sheltered behind their rulers and complained of suffering for another's fault, and this sweeps that shelter away.

The last verse is disputed twice over. Gill and Wesley explain the inhabitant of Lebanon by the cedar houses, and Gill digresses to insist that the mountain has real inhabitants, with villages, a convent and a valley of hermitages, before returning to Jerusalem. Ellicott keeps both senses, the king in his cedar palace having made Lebanon his home, an eagle nesting in the cedars. Calvin takes the words more simply, that they reckoned the mountain an impregnable stronghold and are compared to birds choosing the highest trees for their nests. Then the closing phrase: Ellicott would read it how wilt thou groan, tying it to the pangs that follow; Calvin reports the versions that did so but keeps the received text and reads plain irony, as do Clarke and Wesley; Henry alone hears a forecast of the piety pain produces, humbling and promises of amendment that do not outlast the pangs.
24:
The last king is named in a clipped form, and the voices agree it is deliberate. Calvin calls it a mutilated name, two syllables where the full one has four. Ellicott sets out the three forms the prince bears in scripture and takes the shortest for the name he had before he was proclaimed, so that it carries the same scorn as the private name given his uncle; and the grammar fixes the oracle within the three months of the reign. On the signet the field converges: Ellicott makes the seal-ring the symbol of kingly power that authenticated every edict, Clarke calls it dearer than the finest gem to its owner, Wesley what a man keeps safest; and Gill notes that to swear by one's life is to swear by oneself.

Calvin marks the contrast the sentence turns on: a man plucked from the divine hand into the hand of those who sought his life. On the mother carried with him, Ellicott supposes the king's youth had made her a queen-regent who directed the short reign and shared its fall; Calvin reads her inclusion as added indignity, women and the aged being commonly spared. Of the longing for return, Ellicott says the English loses the force of a Hebrew that has them lifting up their souls to the land; Gill hears either supplication or the false prophets' encouragement.

The question about the broken thing divides them twice. Clarke gives the words to the people, exclaiming when they heard the sentence. Ellicott gives them to the prophet identifying with those who looked on so young a man's doom with wonder and pity, yet pronouncing it inevitable. Calvin has the prophet feigning astonishment at something monstrous so others might cease to wonder; Wesley has him speaking in the person of God. As to what is broken, Gill and Wesley keep the idol, a prince idolised at his accession and now discarded. Ellicott denies the word is the usual one for an idol and would render it a broken piece of handiwork, the image being the potter breaking what his hands made. Calvin takes it for a statue in the proper sense, the verb describing its being loosed from its fastenings, so that broken down is best.

The threefold call to the earth is read for force rather than disputed. Ellicott finds in the repetition the certainty of the decree, and Keil and Delitzsch say it marks what follows as of high importance. Calvin has the hardness of iron overcome by repeated hammer strokes, and insists the vehemence is necessity, not the manner of rhetoricians who aim to seem eloquent. Gill takes the earth as summoned to witness; Clarke hears the prophet answering in his own person over an unhappy and desolated land.

Who is told to write is a third dispute. Gill reports that some address it to angels or prophets, and allows the impersonal, let this man be written childless. Ellicott is precise: it goes to the scribes who kept the royal genealogies, who were to enter the name without waiting for the death; Clarke agrees, the king having sons but no successor. Calvin will have no addressee, taking the phrase from the practice by which lasting decrees were recorded on public tablets, so that the point is permanence. He alone faces the difficulty the sentence raises against the promise of an unbroken line, answering that the childlessness is confined to the interval before Christ: grace was hidden for a time but never extinguished, as the Church was later invisible and yet not dead. Ellicott closes more cautiously, holding it certain that the sceptre departed in this king, since not even Zerubbabel sat on the throne, but doubting whether he died childless in fact, since in these genealogies adoption and levirate marriage so constantly replace parentage that nothing can be inferred.
